Stackhand pricing

Stackhand has two plans. The Free plan monitors up to 3 endpoints with checks every minute. The Team plan costs $29 a month and covers 50 monitors, also checked every minute. There are no hidden fees.

Find themes

Fieldnote's AI theme detection groups quotes from all of your interviews, so you can skip the sticky notes and late-night synthesis sessions. It works whether your research is in one language or 28. When you're ready to share, you can export your themes to Notion or Miro in one click.

No. Quietroom plugs into any standard wall socket. That one connection runs both the ventilation fan and the LED lighting, which together draw 40W. You won't need construction work or contractors, and setting it up won't interrupt your workday.

Reorder alerts

A stockout costs you the sale, and it can cost you the customer too. Crateful's reorder alerts help you restock before that happens. Trips to the clinic can overwhelm a dog or cat. Our four vets come to your living room instead, with a fully equipped portable kit. We handle everything from routine check-ups to blood tests, and blood test results come back within 24 hours. Your pet gets the care it needs at home, without the stress of a clinic visit.

Payroll data is some of the most sensitive information a business holds, so we built security into Paysheet from the start. Every layer of the platform has industry-leading safeguards. Your data is stored in AWS's Cape Town region, encrypted at rest, and handled in strict compliance with the NDPR.

1. Book a free roof assessment. Our team will check how much solar your property can support.
2. We handle the installation, and it's finished in 21 days.

When we launched Patchwork CI, we promised it would always be free for open source. A lot of people told us we were crazy and asked how we'd ever make money.

We now run on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

What surprised me most was the failure data. Across all those repos, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test. That's a lot of developer time spent chasing red builds that weren't real failures.

Open source also gave us feedback and a community along with the users. Our most-requested feature, GitLab support, came straight from OSS maintainers, and we shipped it on November 12. Keeping it free has paid off for us as a business.

#OpenSource #DevOps #CI #DeveloperExperience #BuildInPublic

When we launched Rotaship, we were proud of our mobile app. It was sleek and modern, and we assumed restaurant staff would love it. In the first month, only 12% of them even opened it.

The app was adding a problem instead of solving one. Restaurant teams already live on WhatsApp, and they didn't want another app on their phones.

So in 2025 we made a tough call and moved everything into WhatsApp. We're now in 140 outlets, and the median reply time to shift messages is under 20 minutes.

It's easier to meet people in the tool they already use than to ask them to come to yours. For us, that meant letting go of an app we really liked.

#ProductManagement #Indonesia #StartupLessons #UserExperience

After 11 years working in a clinic, I left. I still loved being a vet, but one part of the job kept getting to me.

Day after day I saw pets so frightened that we had to sedate them just to examine them. I was sure there was a better way to do it.

In 2023 I founded Doorstep Vet. We bring high-quality care to pets at home, where they feel safest.

There are now four of us, and between us we do around 30 home visits a week. The pets are calmer and the owners are happier, and a relaxed animal is much easier to examine properly. Every one of those visits reminds me why I made the jump.

#Veterinary #PetCare #Melbourne #Entrepreneurship #FollowYourPassion

Years ago I was a maintenance engineer at an auto-parts plant in Pune. One day a spindle failed, and the whole production line stopped for three days.

What still bothers me is that we could have seen it coming. Vibration readings had shown the problem two weeks earlier, and no one was watching them.

In 2022 I founded Ferrous to help manufacturers avoid that kind of preventable downtime. Our sensors are now on 410 machines across 17 plants.

#Manufacturing #Industry40 #PredictiveMaintenance #MakeInIndia #StartupStory

Our first production run at Shelfwise went wrong. We shipped 400 labels with a faulty battery contact.

We're a young hardware startup, and there was pressure to cut corners. Instead, we recalled and replaced all 400 labels at our own cost. That set us back about $7,000. It hurt, but customers need to trust that what we ship works, and that was worth the money.

We also added a 100% contact test at the factory. Since then we've shipped 6,000 labels with zero contact failures.

If you're founding a hardware company, you will make mistakes. Own them, fix them fast, and build systems so they don't happen again.

#Hardware #Startups #Manufacturing #Leadership #Integrity

In September we raised Tabwise's price by 50%, from $8 to $12 per user per month. It was one of the scariest decisions we've made.

The reason was simple: our support costs per customer had doubled since launch. We could either cut back on quality or charge enough to cover the work, and we decided to charge more.

We didn't want existing customers to pay for that decision right away, so everyone already on the $8 plan kept that price for 12 months.

In the two months after the change, 2 of our 140 customers churned.

I think the reason is that people buy software for what it does for them, so a fair price increase didn't drive them away. If your costs have grown, it's worth pricing to match.

Founders, when did you last raise your prices?

#SaaS #Pricing #StartupLessons #Growth #B2B

Why we stopped charging a 25% recruiting fee

For years, Northbound Talent charged what every recruiting firm charges: 25% of first-year salary.

It never sat right with me. Our average fee came to about $41,000 per hire, which is a big piece of an early-stage startup's runway. The incentives were also backwards. The higher the salary we negotiated, the more we got paid, and I don't think you can call that a partnership.

In January we switched to a flat $18,000 per hire, with no percentage attached.

This year we've placed 26 senior Rust engineers, and our client relationships are the strongest they've ever been.

I think founders deserve better than the standard model, and I'd like to see more of the industry move this way.

Would you work with a flat-fee recruiter?

Notes on localizing a SaaS product for the Baltics and Nordics, in three parts:
